- If sentiment is consistently low or neutral, model tends to overestimate prices; adjust forecast downward by 1–3% for 30-day horizon.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >5% from prior period), model often overshoots; reduce forecast slope by 10–20% in next 5–7 days.
- When sentiment is positive (e.g., >0.25), model frequently overreacts; cap upward trend at 2–3% above recent peak unless sentiment is strong and sustained.
- If history shows mean reversion (e.g., recent prices oscillating around 75–80), model tends to drift upward; apply downward bias of 2–5% for 10–15 day horizon.
- If model forecast is rising steadily with no recent spike, but true outcome shows sudden drop, check sentiment for negative signals (e.g., 0.00) — reduce forecast slope or add downward correction.
- For 30-day horizon, if true outcome is consistently below model, apply a 3–5% downward adjustment if sentiment is neutral or negative.
- If sentiment is high (e.g., 0.50 or above), model may underreact — increase forecast slightly (1–2%) to reflect sentiment-driven momentum.
- Avoid linear extrapolation after sharp moves — introduce exponential decay or stepwise correction based on sentiment magnitude.
